name: English Standard Version

requestLimits.description: ESV API request ceiling, published by Crossway: 'You may request up to 500 verses per query, or half a book, whichever is less (excepting single-chapter and double-chapter books).' (https://api.esv.org/, retrieved 2026-08-07). ⚠️ CORRECTED 2026-08-07: an earlier version of this note claimed the 'half a book' limit was NOT a request limit and belonged only to the quotation permission. That was wrong — it is stated here, in the API terms, as a per-query limit, and Crossway enforces it server-side. `maxVerses: 500` is therefore only half the rule. The half-book half is not repeated as a value in this block because we do not enforce it here: Crossway's server already truncates a whole-book query, and duplicating the check would produce two error paths for one rule. What their server CANNOT see is a multi-passage study assembling a whole book from individually-compliant queries, so the half-book rule is enforced at study level via restrictions.display instead. The separate '50% of the work in which quoted' clause is a distribution rule and is a genuinely different measurement — see restrictions.distribution. All three axes are laid out in COMPLIANCE.md.

retrieval.description: NO INTERNAL CHUNKING for ESV. One passage = exactly one request, capped at maxVerses. Crossway enforces a PUBLISHED term server-side and silently: 'You may request up to 500 verses per query, or half a book, whichever is less (excepting single-chapter and double-chapter books).' (https://api.esv.org/, retrieved 2026-08-07). A whole-book request returns HTTP 200 with roughly 50% of the verses and a truncated `canonical` field, no error (probed 2026-08-03: Revelation 202/404, Romans 216/433, Galatians 74/149, Ephesians 77/155). The trigger is COMPLETENESS, not size — Romans 1:18-8:39 returns all 208 verses, while the whole book returns 216 of 433. Splitting a whole-book request into sub-whole chunks would return complete text and circumvent a published licence term, so we do not do it: every chunk would succeed and fetchESVPassage()'s truncation detector would never fire. ⚠️ CORRECTED 2026-08-07: this note used to claim there was an unmeasured 'floor somewhere below Galatians' 149'. There is NO floor. Philemon and Jude come back whole because they are SINGLE-CHAPTER books, which the clause above explicitly excepts — not because 25 verses is under some threshold. The six exempt books are Obadiah, Haggai (2 ch), Philemon, 2 John, 3 John and Jude; every other book is capped at half. That exception is now data (`restrictions.display.shortBookChapterThreshold`) and is checked at study-creation time, so the rule no longer relies on Crossway's server to arbitrate — which matters because their server cannot see a MULTI-PASSAGE study that assembles a whole book from compliant queries. `servesCompleteBook: 'partial'` records that some books work and some do not.

caching.quote: You may not locally store more than 500 verses or one-half of any book of the Bible (whichever is less).
caching.recommendation: Periodically clear cache to ensure latest version
caching.description: PUBLISHED ESV API TERM governing LOCAL STORAGE. ⚠️ `maxBookPortion` and `shortBookChapterThreshold` were ADDED 2026-08-10: this block previously held `maxVerses: 500` alone, which transcribed half of its own clause and dropped the other half. The quote above has exactly the shape of the display clause — '500 verses or one-half of any book (whichever is less)' — so storing 400 verses of Galatians (149 total) would have passed a 500-verse-only check while plainly breaching the half-book term. That is the same defect COMPLIANCE.md §1.7 records as 'whichever is less is ONE limit', now found in a third place; `resolveWhicheverIsLess()` exists so the resolution is shared rather than re-derived per call site. The short-book carve-out is inherited from the same sentence pattern the display clause uses, and it matters: the six ≤2-chapter books may be stored whole. Enforced by `planCacheEviction()` (pure) and `enforceCacheLimit()` (writes), triggered after every cache fill.

display.quote: You may not display more than 500 verses or one-half of any book (whichever is less) on any page.
display.description: PUBLISHED ESV API TERM governing DISPLAY, not distribution. Read the quote above carefully: the limit is per PAGE, not per query. That is the whole reason this block has to exist separately from `api.requestLimits`. Crossway enforces the per-query half-book rule server-side by silently truncating (see api.retrieval.description), and for a single passage that enforcement is sufficient — ask for whole Galatians, get 74 of 149 verses. But a study may hold SEVERAL passages, and Galatians 1-3 plus Galatians 4-6 is two individually-compliant queries that together put a complete book on one page. Their server cannot see that; only we can. `validateStudyDisplayLimits()` therefore aggregates coverage per book across all of a study's passages, exactly as `validateExportLimits()` does for exports. `shortBookChapterThreshold: 2` implements the licence's own carve-out — '(excepting single-chapter and double-chapter books)' — which is why Obadiah, Haggai, Philemon, 2 John, 3 John and Jude may be displayed whole while Galatians may not. Those six are the ONLY books the ESV permits displaying in their entirety, and it is also why Crossway's server returns them intact: the exception is in the same clause as the cap. Enforcement is 'warn' by decision, not by licence — see COMPLIANCE.md 'Current posture'.

distribution.cannotExceed: 50% of total work in which quoted
distribution.maxVersesNote: ⚠️ CORRECTED 2026-08-08: was 1000, the PRINT copyright-page permission. The ESV API terms state a lower ceiling for text obtained via the API: 'You may distribute up to 500 verses, as long as the verses quoted do not amount to 50% of a complete book of the Bible and do not make up 50% or more of the total text of the work in which they are quoted.' (https://api.esv.org/, retrieved 2026-08-07). Our text comes from the API, so 500 is the figure that binds us and 1000 was too generous by a factor of two. The earlier note defended leaving it at 1000 on the grounds that `validateExportLimits()` had no caller, so the number 'has no observable effect either way'. That was true when written and stopped being true the moment the check was wired into MenuExport — at which point the app began stating a 1000-verse allowance to users in warning copy. The deferral was sound reasoning resting on a fact that a later change silently removed, which is why COMPLIANCE.md §1.9 records it: a justification that depends on a condition must name the condition, so that whoever removes the condition knows what they have invalidated.
distribution.description: Crossway API quotation permission: up to 500 verses, not amounting to a complete book, and not more than 50% of the work in which quoted. Applies when ESV text leaves the app as a distributable artifact (PNG/PDF/print), not to on-screen study.
distribution.maxBookPortionNote: ⚠️ SUBSTANTIALLY CORRECTED 2026-08-07. The previous note asserted that 'Crossway's permission contains no such rule' as a fraction-of-the-book limit. That is false. The API terms state BOTH measurements in one sentence: 'You may distribute up to 500 verses, as long as the verses quoted do not amount to 50% of a complete book of the Bible AND do not make up 50% or more of the total text of the work in which they are quoted.' (https://api.esv.org/, retrieved 2026-08-07). So there is a real 50%-of-the-BOOK rule and a real 50%-of-the-WORK rule, and the old note argued the first one out of existence by mistaking it for a misreading of the second. The distinction it drew between the two measurements was correct and worth keeping; the conclusion that only one exists was not. This field nevertheless stays null, for a different and narrower reason: `allowCompleteBook: false` already blocks the 100% case, and the 50%-of-book case is caught earlier and more usefully at study level by restrictions.display (an export can only contain what a study displays, so the display check is strictly tighter). Setting it here too would double-report one violation. Revisit if exports ever become possible from a source other than a study. The 50%-of-work clause remains genuinely non-machine-checkable — an Expositor study is mostly Scripture by design — and is carried as a documented obligation in COMPLIANCE.md.

description: The ESV Bible is an essentially literal translation that seeks to reproduce the precise wording of the original text and the personal style of each Bible writer.

translationPhilosophy.summary: An 'essentially literal' translation emphasizing word-for-word correspondence while taking full account of differences in grammar, syntax, and idiom between current literary English and the original languages.
characteristics: Seeks to reproduce the precise wording of the original text
Maintains the personal style of each Bible writer
Transparent to the original text structure and force
Captures echoes and overtones of meaning in original texts
Uses same English word for important recurring words in original
Renders Old Testament passages cited in New Testament to show correspondence
Balances literal precision with readability and literary excellence
strengths: Suitable for public reading and preaching

name: New English Translation

requestLimits.description: SELF-IMPOSED, not a NET API limit. NET publishes no per-request verse ceiling. We cap a single HTTP request at 500 verses as an engineering guardrail so one request stays fast and its response stays a reasonable size. Because `retrieval.chunking` is true, this is NOT a limit on passage size: a passage larger than this is fetched as several sequential requests and stitched back together, so one passage can span a whole book (Psalms = 2,461 verses in 6 requests). It is purely a transport parameter. Because `source` is 'self-imposed', user-facing messages must not attribute this number to the provider. The half-book cap that used to live here was also self-imposed and has been removed — NET's license places no verse limit on distribution. See COMPLIANCE.md.

retrieval.description: INTERNAL CHUNKING ALLOWED for NET. A passage of any size is fetched as however many requests of maxVerses it takes, then concatenated, so passage size is not bounded by request size. This is safe and legitimate here for three reasons: (1) NET's licence explicitly permits complete books (restrictions.distribution.allowCompleteBook = true) and sets no verse limit; (2) the 500-verse request cap is our own engineering guardrail, not a provider rule, so chunking around it routes around nothing; (3) there is no server-side control to circumvent — unlike ESV, the NET API serves whatever range is asked for. Attribution is still mandatory wherever the text appears. Concatenation is safe because wrapWords() derives every data-word-id from absolute book/chapter/verse, so a word's id is identical no matter which chunk delivered it.

display.description: NET places NO limit on how much text may be displayed at once, so every field here is null and `validateStudyDisplayLimits()` returns compliant unconditionally. The block is present rather than omitted so the absence of a limit is explicit and auditable: a missing block would be indistinguishable from an unresearched one. Attribution remains mandatory wherever the text appears. This is why NET is the right choice for whole-book study — Psalms as a single passage is fine here and impossible in ESV.

distribution.description: NET is free to use with attribution and sets no verse or book-portion limit on distribution. Attribution is mandatory wherever the text appears, including exports.

description: The NET Bible is a completely new translation with 60,000+ translator's notes, completed by 25+ scholars working directly from the best available Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek texts.

translationPhilosophy.summary: A balanced translation that overcomes the tension between accuracy and readability, combining faithful rendering of original languages with clear, contemporary English.
characteristics: Faithful to the original biblical languages
Notes explain difficult or nontraditional renderings
Ongoing revisions based on scholarly and user feedback
strengths: Accessible to both academic and general readers
Shows complex linguistic details without sacrificing clarity
Invites readers into the translation process
